items.prompt: Which condition guarantees that the bisection method has a root to find in the interval [a, b]?

options.label: f is differentiable and f'(x) is nonzero everywhere on [a, b]
f is differentiable on [a, b] and f(a) is positive
f is continuous and f(a) equals f(b) at both endpoints
f is continuous and f(a), f(b) have opposite signs

rubric: The intermediate value theorem needs continuity and a sign change between endpoints.
Distractors confuse this with differentiability or derivative conditions used by other methods.

items.prompt: Which formula is the Newton's method update for solving f(x) = 0?

options.label: x_new = x - f(x)/f'(x)
x_new = x + f(x)/f'(x)
x_new = x - f(x)/f''(x)
x_new = x - f'(x)/f(x)

rubric: Newton's update subtracts the function value divided by the derivative.
Distractors flip the ratio, change the sign, or use the second derivative.

items.prompt: On each subinterval, the trapezoidal rule approximates the integrand by which kind of curve?

options.label: A straight line segment
A parabola through three points
A cubic through four points
A constant equal to the midpoint value

rubric: The trapezoidal rule joins endpoint values with a line, forming a trapezoid.
Parabola is Simpson's rule; constant is the midpoint rule.

items.prompt: What is the name of the quantity |exact value - approximate value|?

options.label: Absolute error
Residual
Machine epsilon
Condition number

rubric: Absolute error is the magnitude of the difference between exact and approximate values.
Residual measures how well an approximation satisfies an equation, not distance from the true value.

items.prompt: Gaussian elimination (forward elimination) transforms the matrix of a linear system into which form?

options.label: Diagonal form with unit entries
Upper triangular form
Orthogonal form
Symmetric form

rubric: Forward elimination zeroes entries below the diagonal, giving upper triangular form for back substitution.
Other forms are not produced by elimination alone.

items.prompt: Which of the following are methods for finding roots of an equation f(x) = 0? Select all that apply.

options.label: Bisection method
Simpson's rule
Newton's method
Lagrange interpolation
Secant method

rubric: Bisection, secant and Newton's methods all find roots iteratively.
Simpson's rule is for integration and Lagrange is for interpolation.

items.prompt: A student approximates the derivative of f at x using (f(x+h) - f(x))/h with a small h. Their instructor asks for the name of this formula and the order of its truncation error.

options.label: Forward difference, with error of order h^2
Central difference, with error of order h^2
Backward difference, with error of order h
Forward difference, with error of order h

rubric: The formula uses x+h, so it is a forward difference, first-order accurate with O(h) error.
Distractors mix up the name or the order with the central difference.

items.prompt: Why is bisection described as slow but reliable?

options.label: It fits a parabola to the function, so it can skip over some roots
It uses the slope at each point, so it needs a good starting guess
It halves the bracketing interval each step, so error shrinks steadily
It doubles the correct digits every step, but can diverge from poor guesses

rubric: Halving the bracket gives guaranteed linear convergence once a sign change is bracketed.
Distractors describe Newton-like behaviour or invent a parabola fit.

items.prompt: Why can Newton's method give a huge, wild step when f'(x_n) is nearly zero?

options.label: Dividing by a tiny slope makes the tangent's root very far away
Round-off makes the computed derivative negative, so each step reverses direction
The tangent becomes almost vertical, so it meets the axis very near x_n
The function value f(x_n) must also be near zero, so the step overshoots

rubric: A nearly flat tangent crosses the x-axis far from x_n, so the step f/f' is huge.
A vertical tangent would correspond to a very large slope, not a small one.

items.prompt: Why is Simpson's rule usually more accurate than the trapezoidal rule for smooth functions with the same step size?

options.label: It fits parabolas, not lines, so its error shrinks like h^4
It uses the exact derivative of f at every node, so slope errors cancel
It samples the function at randomly placed points, so errors average out
It leaves out the endpoints, which are the least accurate samples

rubric: Quadratic fits capture curvature, giving O(h^4) error versus O(h^2) for trapezoid.
Distractors invent randomness, derivative use, or dropping endpoints.

items.prompt: The composite trapezoidal rule has error proportional to h^2. If you halve the step size h for a smooth function, what happens to the error roughly?

options.label: It stays about the same
It is cut roughly in half
It is cut by a factor of about 4
It is cut by a factor of about 16

rubric: Error proportional to h^2 drops by (1/2)^2 = 1/4 when h is halved.
Halving would be for first-order methods; 16 is for fourth-order methods like Simpson's.

items.prompt: Why does Gaussian elimination usually use partial pivoting?

options.label: It guarantees the computed solution is exact in floating point
It avoids dividing by tiny pivots that magnify round-off
It makes the matrix symmetric, so fewer elimination steps are needed
It cuts the operation count from order n^3 to order n^2 per solve

rubric: Choosing the largest pivot keeps multipliers small and limits round-off growth.
Pivoting doesn't reduce cost order or make arithmetic exact.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain sources of round-off error on a computer? Select all that apply.

options.label: A number like 0.1 has no exact finite binary floating-point representation
Round-off error disappears if you run more iterations of any method
Subtracting two nearly equal numbers can lose many significant digits
Using a smaller step size h always reduces the total error of a finite-difference formula

rubric: Cancellation and non-representable decimals are both genuine round-off sources.
Very small h can increase round-off, and extra iterations do not remove it.

items.prompt: A student estimates f'(1) for f(x) = sin(x) using (f(x+h) - f(x))/h. With h = 1e-6 the answer is accurate to about 6 digits, but with h = 1e-14 it is much worse. What best explains the worse result?

options.label: Subtracting nearly equal values loses digits, so round-off dominates
Truncation error grows as h shrinks, so the approximation worsens
The formula is only valid for steps larger than about 1e-6, so it breaks
Sine is not differentiable at such tiny steps, so the limit fails

rubric: For tiny h, f(x+h) and f(x) agree to nearly all digits, so cancellation causes large round-off error.
Truncation error actually shrinks with h; the formula remains valid.

items.prompt: Which condition guarantees that the bisection method has a root to find in the starting interval [a, b]?

options.label: f is differentiable on [a,b] and f'(a), f'(b) have opposite signs
f is continuous on [a,b] and f(a), f(b) have opposite signs
f is continuous on [a,b] and |f(a)| is smaller than |f(b)|
f is increasing on [a,b] and f(a), f(b) are both positive

rubric: Continuity plus a sign change lets the intermediate value theorem guarantee a root in the interval.
Distractors confuse the sign of the derivative or the size of the function values with a sign change of f.

items.prompt: The forward difference (f(x+h) - f(x))/h approximates f'(x). The error caused by dropping the higher-order terms in the expansion of f(x+h) is called what?

options.label: Overflow error, from numbers exceeding the largest float
Absolute error, from the size of the step h chosen
Truncation error, from cutting off an infinite expansion
Round-off error, from storing numbers with finite digits

rubric: Truncation error comes from replacing an infinite or exact process by a finite approximation.
Round-off error stems from finite-precision storage, not from the formula itself.

items.prompt: Newton's method is started close to a simple root of a smooth function. What does quadratic convergence mean for its behaviour?

options.label: The error shrinks by about half at each iteration, as in bisection
The error stays fixed once the guess is close enough
One extra correct digit is gained at each iteration, steadily
The number of correct digits roughly doubles each iteration

rubric: Quadratic convergence means the new error is about proportional to the square of the old error, so correct digits roughly double.
Halving the error or gaining one digit describes linear convergence, as in bisection.

items.prompt: How does the composite trapezoidal rule approximate the integral of f over [a, b]?

options.label: It replaces f on each subinterval by a straight line segment
It replaces f by one polynomial passing through all the nodes
It replaces f on each subinterval by a constant equal to the left value
It replaces f on each subinterval by a parabola through three points

rubric: The trapezoidal rule joins neighbouring points with straight lines and sums the trapezoid areas.
Parabolas describe Simpson's rule and constants describe rectangle rules.

items.prompt: A linear system Ax = b has a matrix A with a very large condition number. What does this tell you?

options.label: The solution vector is too large to be stored in floating point
The matrix is exactly singular and the system has no solution at all
Small relative changes in the data can cause large relative changes in the solution
The elimination algorithm is unstable, so switching to another algorithm will remove the sensitivity

rubric: The condition number measures sensitivity of the problem itself, regardless of algorithm.
A common misconception is that a large condition number means an algorithm flaw or exact singularity.

items.prompt: Which statements about error in numerical computation are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: Making the step h smaller in a finite difference always reduces the total error
Halving h in a second-order method cuts the truncation error by about a factor of 4
Subtracting two nearly equal numbers can lose many significant digits
Floating-point arithmetic stores decimal fractions such as 0.1 exactly

rubric: Cancellation loses digits, and second-order truncation error scales with h^2, so halving h gives about a quarter.
Very small h increases round-off error, and 0.1 has no exact binary representation.

items.prompt: A student solves a 3x3 linear system with Gaussian elimination and no row swapping. The top-left entry is 1e-12 while other entries are near 1, and the computed answer is far from the true solution. The student asks why this happened.

options.label: Gaussian elimination is only valid for symmetric matrices, so the method breaks down on a nonsymmetric input like this one
The right-hand side is too large, so dividing the whole system by its largest entry would fix the pivot and the error
The tiny pivot gives huge multipliers that amplify round-off error, so swapping rows for a larger pivot helps
The matrix must be singular, because any tiny pivot means the determinant is exactly zero and no solution exists

rubric: Dividing by a tiny pivot creates huge multipliers that magnify round-off; partial pivoting avoids this.
Distractors wrongly blame singularity, symmetry or scaling of the right-hand side.

items.prompt: Bisection is applied to f(x) = x^2 - 2 on [1, 2]. What is the new interval after one step?
rubric: The midpoint is 1.5 and f(1.5) = 0.25 > 0, which matches the sign of f(2), so the root lies in [1, 1.5].
Choosing [1.5, 2] comes from keeping the wrong side of the sign change.

items.prompt: Apply one Newton iteration to f(x) = x^2 - 9 starting from x0 = 6. What is x1?
rubric: Other values come from using the wrong derivative or forgetting to divide by f'.

items.prompt: Use the composite trapezoidal rule with n = 2 subintervals to approximate the integral of x^2 from 0 to 2. What value results?
rubric: 8/3 is the exact integral, and the other values come from dropping the factor 2 on the middle point.

items.prompt: Use Simpson's rule with n = 2 subintervals to approximate the integral of x^3 from 0 to 2. What value results?
rubric: Using weights 1, 2, 1 or the wrong factor h/2 gives the other values.

items.prompt: Use the forward difference with h = 0.1 to approximate the derivative of f(x) = x^2 at x = 3. What value results?
rubric: 6.0 is the exact derivative or central difference value, and 5.9 comes from a backward-style slip.

items.prompt: Bisection is to be started on [0, 1]. For which functions can it be applied directly and be guaranteed to find a root? Select all that apply.

options.label: f(x) = cos(x) - x

rubric: Both are continuous with f(0) and f(1) of opposite signs.
x^2 + 1 has no sign change, and 1/(x - 0.5) changes sign only through a discontinuity, not a root.

items.prompt: A sensor logs a temperature of 14 C at 2:00 and 20 C at 4:00, with no readings in between. An engineer uses linear interpolation between these two points to estimate the temperature at 3:30.
rubric: The fraction of the interval is 1.5/2 = 0.75, so T = 14 + 0.75 * 6 = 18.5.
17.0 and 18.0 come from using the wrong fraction of the interval, and 19.0 from misreading the time.

items.prompt: Apply two Newton iterations to `f(x) = x^2 - 2` starting at `x0 = 1`. What is `x2`?
rubric: 1.5 is only x1; 1.41421 is the true root, not the second iterate.

items.prompt: Bisection is applied to `f(x) = x^3 - x - 2` on [1, 2]. After two iterations, which interval is known to contain the root?
rubric: [1.5, 2] is the interval after only one iteration.

items.prompt: Use the composite trapezoid rule with n = 4 subintervals to approximate the integral of `x^2` from 0 to 2. What value results?
rubric: 2.667 is the exact value; 5.5 forgets to multiply by h.

items.prompt: For `f(x) = x^3`, use the central difference with h = 0.1 to approximate `f'(1)`. Which value do you get?
rubric: 3.31 is the forward difference result, and 2.71 is the backward difference result.

items.prompt: A quadratic polynomial interpolates the points (0, 1), (1, 3) and (2, 7). What value does it give at x = 3?
rubric: The interpolant is 1 + x + x^2, so p(3) = 13.
11 comes from extrapolating linearly with the last slope pattern of the data, ignoring the quadratic term.

items.prompt: Bisection needs a bracket where `f(a)` and `f(b)` have opposite signs. For `f(x) = x^2 - 3`, which intervals are valid starting brackets? Select all that apply.
rubric: f(1) = -2 and f(2) = 1 differ in sign; f(-2) = 1 and f(0) = -3 differ in sign.
The other intervals have the same sign at both ends, even though [-1, 1] and others may look symmetric.

items.prompt: A simulation must solve `Ax = b` for 500 different right-hand sides `b`, always with the same dense 2000 x 2000 matrix `A`. You want the lowest total cost while staying accurate. Which approach should you implement?

options.label: Factor `A = LU` with pivoting once, then do forward and back substitution for each `b`
Run Gaussian elimination from scratch for each `b`, because each system is then solved independently
Apply Cramer's rule with determinants for each `b`, because it gives an exact formula for every component
Use Jacobi iteration for every `b`, because iterative methods always cost less than direct methods

rubric: The O(n^3) factorisation is paid once and each solve costs only O(n^2).
Re-eliminating repeats the O(n^3) work, and Cramer's rule is far costlier; Jacobi needs convergence conditions that are not given.

items.prompt: Newton's method on `f(x) = x^3 - 2x + 2` from `x0 = 0` gives 0, 1, 0, 1, ... What explains this behaviour?

options.label: The root is a multiple root, so convergence is only linear and the iterates stall near 0 and 1
Round-off error accumulates at each step and pushes the iterates back toward the starting value
The derivative is zero at x0 = 0, so the first step is undefined and the code returns the start again
The Newton step from 0 lands at 1 and the step from 1 lands at 0, so the iterates form a 2-cycle

rubric: f'(0) = -2 gives x1 = 1, and f(1) = 1, f'(1) = 1 gives x2 = 0, a cycle.
f'(0) is not zero, and the pattern is exact, not caused by round-off or multiplicity.

items.prompt: A program computes `(1 - cos(x)) / x^2` in double precision. At `x = 1e-8` it returns 0 instead of about 0.5. What is the cause?

options.label: Subtracting two nearly equal numbers cancels almost all significant digits
Truncation error from stopping the Taylor series of cosine after too few terms
Overflow when dividing by the very small quantity `x^2` in floating point
An ill-conditioned input that makes every algorithm unstable for this function

rubric: cos(1e-8) rounds to 1, so the subtraction yields 0: catastrophic cancellation.
The function is well-conditioned; a rewrite such as 2 sin^2(x/2)/x^2 avoids the problem.

items.prompt: A forward-difference derivative approximation has error 5e-2 at h = 0.1 and 2.5e-2 at h = 0.05. What do these data indicate about the method's order?

options.label: Second order, since the error shrinks as h gets smaller
Fourth order, since the error is small at both step sizes
Round-off dominated, since the error does not fall by a factor of 4
First order, since halving h halves the error

rubric: Error proportional to h means halving h halves the error: first order.
Second order would give a factor of 4; round-off domination would show the error growing as h shrinks.

items.prompt: Gaussian elimination without pivoting on `[[1e-20, 1], [1, 1]] x = [1, 2]` in double precision gives a badly wrong answer. What is the cause?

options.label: The right-hand side has too few significant digits for the system to be solved accurately
The tiny pivot gives a multiplier of 1e20 that swamps the other entries and loses information
The matrix is nearly singular, so its condition number is huge and any method, even with row swaps, fails
The matrix is not diagonally dominant, so elimination cannot finish without switching to an iterative method

rubric: A multiplier of 1e20 makes the updated entries lose the original data; row swapping fixes it.
The matrix is well-conditioned (condition number near 2.6), so this is an algorithm instability, not an ill-conditioned problem.

items.prompt: A degree-10 polynomial interpolates `1/(1 + 25x^2)` at 11 equally spaced points on [-1, 1]. It fits well in the middle but oscillates wildly near the ends. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: Equally spaced nodes make the node-polynomial factor in the error large near the ends (Runge phenomenon)
Too few nodes were used, so adding more equally spaced nodes will steadily reduce the end error
Round-off in the Lagrange formula is amplified, so a higher-precision type would remove the oscillations
The function has a jump, so no polynomial can approximate it well on any set of nodes

rubric: With equal spacing the factor product(x - xi) is largest near the endpoints, and the error grows with degree for this function.
The function is smooth, and more equispaced nodes make the oscillation worse; Chebyshev nodes help.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe a linear system `Ax = b` with a very large condition number for `A`? Select all that apply.

options.label: A tiny relative change in `b` can cause a large relative change in the solution `x`
The computed solution can lose many digits even when the elimination is backward stable
Partial pivoting removes the ill-conditioning by changing the system's sensitivity
A tiny residual `||b - Ax_computed||` guarantees that `x_computed` is accurate

rubric: Sensitivity to perturbations is what condition number measures, and it limits accuracy even for stable algorithms.
A small residual does not imply a small error here, and pivoting improves stability, not the conditioning of the problem.

items.prompt: A student applies composite Simpson's rule to the integral of `sqrt(x)` from 0 to 1, doubling n each time. The error shrinks by only about 2.8 per doubling, not the 16 expected for a fourth-order rule. The code's weights (1, 4, 2, 4, ..., 4, 1) are correct. What is the most likely reason?

options.label: Simpson's rule needs n to be a multiple of 4, so every second doubling gives an invalid, less accurate rule
The fourth derivative of `sqrt(x)` is unbounded at 0, so the usual error bound fails
The interior weights are miscounted in the code, which silently lowers the order of the rule
Round-off error dominates at these step sizes, so halving h no longer reduces the total error

rubric: The singular behaviour at x = 0 reduces the convergence to about h^1.5, a factor near 2.8 per halving.
The weights are stated to be correct, an even n suffices, and round-off would not give a steady factor of 2.8.

items.prompt: Newton's method is applied to f(x) = x^3 - 2x + 2 with x0 = 0. The iterates alternate 0, 1, 0, 1, ... and never converge. Which diagnosis is correct?

options.label: The second derivative is negative at both points, which flips the sign of every update and blocks convergence
The tangent at x=0 meets the axis at x=1 and the tangent at x=1 meets it at x=0, so the iteration is trapped in a 2-cycle
Since f'(0) equals zero, the first step divides by zero and every later iterate is only a rounding artifact
The function has no real root, so Newton's method is forced to oscillate instead of converging to anything

rubric: f(0)=2, f'(0)=-2 gives x1=1, and f(1)=1, f'(1)=1 gives x2=0, so the iteration is a genuine 2-cycle.
Distractors misstate the facts: f'(0) is -2, a real root exists near -1.77, and f'' is 0 and 6 at the two points.

items.prompt: A forward difference (f(x+h)-f(x))/h for f = sin at x = 1 is computed in double precision. The error falls as h goes from 1e-1 to about 1e-8, then rises as h goes down to 1e-15. What explains the rise?

options.label: The truncation term h f''(x)/2 starts to grow once h falls below the square root of machine epsilon
Division by a very small h is itself inexact, which adds an error proportional to h to the computed quotient
Cancellation in f(x+h)-f(x) leaves few correct digits, and dividing by a tiny h magnifies that rounding error
Higher derivatives of sin become unbounded as h shrinks, so the Taylor remainder stops being a small quantity

rubric: Rounding error of size about eps/h from subtractive cancellation grows as h shrinks while truncation error falls.
Distractors wrongly claim truncation error grows or that derivatives of sin blow up.

items.prompt: Gaussian elimination without row exchanges is applied to [[1e-20, 1],[1, 1]] x = [1, 2] in double precision. It returns x1 = 0, although the true x1 is about 1. What is the cause?

options.label: Double precision cannot represent 1e-20, so the entry is stored as zero and the system becomes singular
The multiplier 1e20 fills the updated second row with huge entries, so the original information is rounded away
Back substitution divides by the smallest entry first, so errors pile up there whatever the pivot order is
The matrix is singular to working precision, so no algorithm could recover x1 to any useful accuracy

rubric: A tiny pivot gives a giant multiplier and element growth, which swamps the other entries; partial pivoting avoids this.
The matrix has a small condition number and 1e-20 is representable, so the other options misdiagnose the failure.

items.prompt: Composite Simpson's rule on the integral of sqrt(x) over [0, 1] shows error falling only like h^1.5 rather than h^4. Which analysis explains this?

options.label: The derivative of sqrt(x) is unbounded at 0, so the fourth-derivative error bound fails and the first panel dominates the error
Rounding error in sqrt grows with the number of panels, so roundoff rather than truncation dominates the total error
An even number of subintervals makes the weights 4 and 2 misalign for non-periodic functions, reducing the order
Simpson's rule drops two orders of accuracy on any integrand that is not a polynomial of degree three or less

rubric: The h^4 order assumes a bounded fourth derivative; the endpoint singularity breaks that and limits the rate.
Other options invent order loss for all non-polynomials or blame roundoff, which would not give a clean h^1.5 rate.

items.prompt: Solving H x = b for the 12x12 Hilbert matrix by LU with partial pivoting gives a residual near 1e-16 times norm(b), yet the computed x has almost no correct digits. What explains this?

options.label: H is badly ill-conditioned, so a tiny residual is compatible with a large error; error can reach cond(H) times the relative residual
Hilbert matrices are singular in exact arithmetic, so the system has no unique solution and any computed answer is essentially arbitrary
The residual is computed in the same precision as the solve, so rounding hides the true error and it always looks small whatever the error is
Partial pivoting is unstable on symmetric positive definite matrices, so the solver reports a misleadingly small residual for a wrong answer

rubric: Forward error is bounded by cond(A) times relative residual, and cond of the 12x12 Hilbert matrix is around 1e16.
Distractors blame pivoting or singularity; Hilbert matrices are nonsingular and pivoted LU is backward stable.

items.prompt: The quadratic formula in double precision is used for x^2 - 1e8 x + 1 = 0. The larger root is accurate but the smaller root (about 1e-8) has few correct digits. Which statements explain this? Select all that apply.

options.label: For the small root, -b + sqrt(b^2 - 4ac) subtracts two nearly equal numbers, cancelling leading digits
The small root is inherently ill-conditioned in b, so no formula could compute it accurately
The computed discriminant becomes negative through rounding, so the small root comes from a complex pair
The large root also suffers cancellation, but its larger magnitude hides the lost digits
The subtraction's absolute rounding error is about eps times 1e8, which is huge next to a root of size 1e-8

rubric: Cancellation leaves an absolute error near eps*1e8, which overwhelms a root of size 1e-8.
The discriminant stays positive, the large root adds same-sign terms, and the small root is well conditioned (c/(a*large root) works).

items.prompt: An analyst interpolates f(x) = 1/(1+25x^2) on [-1, 1] with one degree-14 polynomial through 15 equally spaced points. The fit is excellent near the centre but oscillates wildly near x = ±1, and adding more equispaced points makes it worse. Which explanation is correct?

options.label: The function is discontinuous at its peak, so the interpolation error bound is infinite for every possible node placement
Rounding error in the Vandermonde system dominates, so solving the same problem in exact arithmetic would make the interpolants converge
The node polynomial grows rapidly near the ends for equispaced nodes, and the poles of f at ±i/5 prevent the interpolants from converging
Polynomial interpolation of an even function loses its symmetry, and that asymmetry shows up as error at the endpoints

rubric: This is the Runge phenomenon: equispaced nodes plus complex singularities near the interval make the interpolation error grow with degree.
The function is smooth and the divergence occurs even in exact arithmetic, so roundoff and discontinuity explanations fail.

items.prompt: You must find a root of a smooth function whose evaluations cost minutes and whose derivative is unavailable. A sign-changing bracket is known. The method must never diverge and should converge faster than bisection. Which is best?

options.label: Brent's method, which takes interpolation steps when safe and falls back to bisection to keep the bracket
Fixed-point iteration on x = x + f(x), because it avoids both a derivative and the need for any bracketing
The secant method started from the bracket ends, because it is superlinear and needs one evaluation per step
Newton's method with a finite-difference derivative, because quadratic convergence minimises the number of expensive evaluations

rubric: Brent's method keeps a guaranteed bracket while usually converging superlinearly, meeting both criteria.
Newton with finite differences and secant lack a convergence guarantee, and the fixed-point form need not contract.

items.prompt: You must integrate an analytic, non-oscillatory function over [0, 1] to absolute error 1e-12. Each function evaluation takes seconds, so the number of evaluations is the main cost. Which method best meets this?

options.label: Gauss–Legendre quadrature with a modest number of nodes, because its error decays geometrically in the node count
Monte Carlo with 1e6 random samples, because its error does not depend on how smooth the integrand is at all
Composite trapezoid rule with 1e6 uniform panels, because its weights are all positive and the rule is therefore robust
Composite Simpson's rule with step halving until estimates agree, because it is O(h^4) and reuses all earlier evaluations

rubric: Gauss rules converge exponentially for analytic integrands, so few expensive evaluations reach 1e-12.
Trapezoid and Simpson need far more evaluations, and Monte Carlo error is about 1e-3 at 1e6 samples.

items.prompt: A 2D Poisson discretisation gives a sparse symmetric positive definite system with 4 million unknowns on a machine with 16 GB of RAM. A relative residual of 1e-8 is required. Which approach best meets these criteria?

options.label: An explicit inverse from Gauss–Jordan elimination, since the inverse can be reused for later right-hand sides
Dense LU with partial pivoting, since it is backward stable and delivers the answer in a fixed number of steps
Preconditioned conjugate gradients, since it needs only sparse products and a few vectors
Jacobi iteration, since each sweep costs one sparse product and the sweep count stays small as the grid is refined

rubric: Preconditioned CG fits in memory and converges in far fewer iterations than stationary methods for SPD systems.
Dense storage of 4 million unknowns would need about 128 TB, and Jacobi's iteration count grows as the grid is refined.

items.prompt: A degree-9 polynomial least-squares fit to 200 points has a design matrix A with cond(A) about 1e7 in double precision (eps about 1e-16). You need at least 6 correct digits in the coefficients. Which method best meets this?

options.label: Cholesky on the normal equations, since forming A^T A reduces the problem to a small symmetric system that is solved stably
Gaussian elimination on 10 chosen rows, since a square system is more stable than an overdetermined one
Normal equations with iterative refinement in double precision, since refinement restores full accuracy whatever the conditioning
Householder QR on A, since the error scales with cond(A), about 1e7, rather than with its square

rubric: QR error is about cond(A)*eps, near 1e-9, which meets the 6-digit target.
Normal equations have condition about 1e14 and leave almost no digits; refinement in the same precision does not fix that.

items.prompt: A colleague stops Newton's method on f(x) = (x-1)^3 when |x_{k+1} - x_k| < 1e-10 and claims the error is below 1e-10. Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: Sound: the step size bounds the error for any iteration, since the error equals the distance moved in the final step
Flawed: at a triple root Newton is only linear with ratio 2/3, so the error is about twice the step, near 2e-10
Sound: Newton's method is quadratically convergent, so the error is always far smaller than the last step taken
Flawed: at a multiple root Newton's iterates stall away from the root, so a tiny step says nothing about closeness to x = 1

rubric: For multiplicity 3 the error ratio is 2/3, so step = e/3 and the remaining error is about 2 times the step.
Newton converges (linearly) at multiple roots, and a small step bounds the error only when convergence is fast.

items.prompt: You must interpolate 30 equispaced samples of a smooth function and then evaluate the result at arbitrary points. Which are sound reasons to prefer a cubic spline to one degree-29 polynomial? Select all that apply.

options.label: The spline coefficients come from a tridiagonal system, so construction costs O(n) rather than a dense solve
Local cubic pieces avoid the endpoint oscillation seen with high-degree equispaced polynomial interpolation
For smooth functions the spline error shrinks like h^4 as samples are added, while the polynomial can get worse
The spline passes through more of the data points than the polynomial, which can match at most 15 points
The spline has continuous derivatives of every order, so it reproduces any smooth function exactly between nodes

rubric: Splines avoid Runge oscillation, cost O(n) via a tridiagonal solve, and give O(h^4) error for smooth data.
A cubic spline is only C2 and not exact between nodes, and both interpolants pass through all 30 points.

items.prompt: A sensor gives position samples every 0.01 s with random noise of about 1e-3 units, and the true motion is smooth with moderate acceleration. You must estimate velocity with the lowest overall error. Which option best meets this goal?

options.label: Interpolate to spacing 0.001 and take central differences, because the smaller h reduces the truncation error of the derivative
Fit low-degree polynomials over a sliding window of samples and differentiate the fit, trading a little bias for far less noise amplification
Apply Richardson extrapolation to central differences at spacings 0.01 and 0.02, because removing the leading error term gives the best derivative
Use a 7-point high-order difference stencil, because truncation error falls with stencil order and random noise averages out

rubric: Differencing amplifies noise by about 1/h, so local least-squares smoothing (Savitzky–Golay style) gives the best bias–variance balance.
Higher-order stencils, extrapolation and finer interpolated spacing do not reduce measurement noise and can amplify it.

items.prompt: Newton's method is applied to f(x) = x^3 - 2x + 2 from x0 = 0. The iterates alternate 0, 1, 0, 1, ... Which judgement about a production root finder is best supported?

options.label: Rounding error causes the oscillation, so switching to extended precision would fix it
The iteration converges slowly to the root, so a tighter tolerance will eventually succeed
Newton is trapped in a 2-cycle here, so the solver needs a bracketing or damped fallback
A multiple root at x = 0 causes linear convergence, so deflation is the right remedy

rubric: Newton maps 0 to 1 and 1 back to 0 exactly, a genuine cycle independent of precision or tolerance.
Distractors confuse cycling with slow convergence, multiple roots, or rounding.

items.prompt: A colleague claims Simpson's rule is always more accurate than the trapezoid rule on the same nodes. Evaluate this for a smooth analytic periodic function integrated over one full period.

options.label: The claim holds: Simpson's error is O(h^4) against O(h^2), so it wins for every smooth integrand
The claim fails: both rules are exact for periodic functions, because the oscillating parts integrate to zero
The claim holds: trapezoid error always stays O(h^2), because Euler-Maclaurin corrections never cancel
The claim fails: the trapezoid rule converges geometrically there, because endpoint error terms cancel by periodicity

rubric: Euler-Maclaurin endpoint terms cancel for periodic integrands, giving spectral convergence for the trapezoid rule.
Distractors apply order-of-accuracy rules blindly or overstate exactness.

items.prompt: A solver returns x_hat for Ax = b with a relative residual of 1e-16, and cond(A) = 1e12. Which is the best judgement of the relative error in x_hat?

options.label: It is about 1e-28, because the residual and the conditioning multiply to shrink error
It is about 1e-16, because a tiny residual means the solution is equally accurate
It is exactly zero, because a backward stable solver returns the exact solution
It may be as large as about 1e-4, because error can grow with cond(A) times the residual

rubric: Forward error can reach roughly cond(A) times the relative residual, here about 1e-4.
Distractors equate small residual with small error or misuse backward stability.

items.prompt: You estimate f'(x) with (f(x+h) - f(x))/h in double precision, where f and its derivatives are of order 1 near x. Which h gives the smallest total error?

options.label: 1e-8, balancing truncation error against rounding error
1e-16, since truncation error vanishes as h shrinks
1e-12, since rounding error is negligible there
1e-4, since rounding error dominates below that

rubric: Truncation error ~h and rounding error ~eps/h balance near h = sqrt(eps), about 1e-8.
Distractors ignore the growth of rounding error as h shrinks.

items.prompt: You need the integral of cos(x)/sqrt(x) over [0,1] to 1e-10 with the fewest function evaluations. Which approach is the best judged choice?

options.label: Gauss-Legendre with 20 nodes directly in x, since the integrand is smooth elsewhere
Substitute x = t^2 to get a smooth integrand, then apply Gauss-Legendre in t
Trapezoid rule with Richardson extrapolation, since it cancels the singular term
Composite Simpson with 1e6 equal panels, skipping the sample at x = 0

rubric: The substitution gives 2cos(t^2), which is analytic, so Gauss-Legendre converges rapidly.
Distractors apply high-order rules to an endpoint singularity, which ruins their convergence.

items.prompt: A teammate solves Ax = b for a large sparse nonsingular A by computing inv(A) explicitly and then x = inv(A)*b. Which criticisms are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Nonsingular matrices have no inverse in floating point, so the code cannot run
Factorizations cannot be reused across right-hand sides, so the inverse is needed
Forming the inverse costs more operations than a single factorization and solve
The inverse of a sparse matrix is usually dense, wasting memory and time
The computed x is typically no more accurate than, and often worse than, a direct solve

rubric: Explicit inversion costs more, destroys sparsity, and gives no accuracy gain over a factorization-based solve.
Distractors claim inverses cannot be computed or that factorizations cannot be reused, both false.

items.prompt: An adaptive quadrature routine integrates a function whose value is about 1e8. The team sets an absolute tolerance of 1e-10, and the routine hits its maximum subdivision depth without converging. Double precision is used. Which judgement is best?

options.label: The depth limit is too low, so raise it until the absolute tolerance is met
The tolerance is below attainable rounding error (about 1e-8), so use a relative tolerance
The routine's error estimator is biased, so replace it with a higher-order rule on each panel
The integrand must have a singularity, so switch to a random sampling method

rubric: With value 1e8 and eps near 1e-16, absolute accuracy better than about 1e-8 is unattainable; relative tolerance is appropriate.
Distractors blame the estimator, depth, or a singularity instead of floating-point limits.

items.prompt: Design a root finder for a continuous f with a known sign change on [a,b]. Constraints: guaranteed convergence, typically superlinear speed, and no derivative available. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: Newton's method using a finite-difference derivative, started at the midpoint of the bracket
Brent's method, mixing bisection with secant and inverse quadratic steps in a bracket
Plain bisection, halving the bracket each step until its width falls below the tolerance
Unbracketed secant iteration, started from the two endpoints and run until the step is small

rubric: Brent's method keeps a bracket for guaranteed convergence and uses interpolation steps for superlinear speed without derivatives.
Distractors drop either the guarantee (Newton, secant) or the speed (bisection).

items.prompt: Design a routine for log(1+x) accurate to near full double precision for every x in [0,1], including x near 1e-12, using only log and basic arithmetic. Which design meets this?

options.label: Set u = 1 + x; if u == 1 return x, else return log(u) * x / (u - 1)
Use the three-term Taylor series x - x^2/2 + x^3/3 for all x
Compute log(1 + x) in single precision, then refine by one Newton step
Compute log(1 + x) directly, since log is correctly rounded

rubric: The correction x/(u-1) compensates for rounding in u = 1 + x, keeping accuracy at all scales.
Direct evaluation loses digits for tiny x, and a short Taylor series fails near x = 1.

items.prompt: Design a plan for a dense, nonsymmetric 2000 x 2000 system A x = b where A is fixed and 500 different right-hand sides arrive one at a time. Which plan is best?

options.label: Form inv(A) once, then multiply it by each right-hand side to get every solution vector
Run LU with partial pivoting once, then do two triangular solves per right-hand side
Run Gaussian elimination without pivoting on every new system, since skipping row swaps saves work
Run Cholesky once, then reuse its factor for each right-hand side with two triangular solves

rubric: One pivoted LU factorization costs O(n^3) and each later solve costs O(n^2), stable for general A.
Cholesky needs a symmetric positive definite matrix; the other options cost more or lose stability.

items.prompt: Design a quadrature for f over [0,2] where f is smooth except for a derivative jump at the known point x = 0.7. The target is 1e-10 using a high-order rule. Which design works?

options.label: Apply Gauss-Legendre on [0,0.7] and [0.7,2] separately, so each piece is smooth
Use a composite trapezoid rule on [0,2] with a very small step
Apply one high-order Gauss-Legendre rule over [0,2], since f is continuous
Apply Simpson's rule on [0,2] with a node placed near 0.7

rubric: Splitting at the kink makes each subinterval analytic so Gauss-Legendre converges rapidly.
A single rule across the kink loses its high-order convergence.

items.prompt: Design an interpolant through monotone increasing data points. Constraints: it must be monotone between nodes, and its first derivative must be continuous. Which choice meets both?

options.label: Piecewise linear interpolation, since it is monotone on every interval
A single polynomial through all points, since it is infinitely smooth
A natural cubic spline, since it is C2 and therefore smooth enough
A monotone piecewise cubic Hermite interpolant (PCHIP) with limited slopes

rubric: PCHIP limits node slopes to enforce monotonicity while remaining C1.
Splines and global polynomials can overshoot; linear interpolation has discontinuous derivatives.

items.prompt: A proposed adaptive Simpson integrator sometimes loops forever or returns results missing the tolerance. Which additions make it terminate and meet its tolerance sensibly? Select all that apply.

options.label: Halve the tolerance and never subdivide, to save evaluations
Use tolerance = max(abs_tol, rel_tol * |estimated integral|)
Estimate panel error by comparing one Simpson step with two half-width steps
Cap the recursion depth and report failure if the cap is reached
Accept a panel whenever the midpoint function value is below the tolerance

rubric: A depth cap guarantees termination, a combined tolerance respects floating point limits, and the comparison gives an error estimate.
Midpoint size says nothing about integration error, and never subdividing cannot meet tolerance.

items.prompt: A 1 kHz sensor stream has a smooth signal plus noise of amplitude 1e-3. You must estimate the signal's first derivative in real time. A central difference with h = 1 ms gives noise of order 1, swamping the signal. Which design best satisfies the need to suppress noise while keeping the derivative accurate?

options.label: Use a one-sided forward difference, since it avoids the subtractive cancellation of a central difference
Use a high-order finite-difference stencil over the nearest 3 samples only, to cut truncation error
Use a smaller step by interpolating the stream to 100 kHz before differencing adjacent points
Fit a local low-degree polynomial over a sliding window and differentiate it

rubric: A sliding-window least-squares polynomial fit averages noise while preserving the smooth signal's derivative.
Smaller steps or short stencils amplify noise further, and forward differences are no less noisy.
